snippet.textDisplay: Driving: we let the Dr. be the bad guy (and we make sure we are available to take her where she wants to go). When she complains about not driving, we just remind her that the doctor said no. (He actually looked at her test results and used that to make a decision.) Looking out for when they are tired: Yes, we have learned to schedule for this! We try not to have her do too many things in one day or do things too late in the day. It was definitely a learning curve, but now that we have the rhythm of it, she is doing so much better because we try to get her home before she is too worn out, and once she gets home she relaxes. We can tell when her brain starts to "shut down" when we are out. It's not like we are out all the time...she goes to the doctor and shopping mostly. Unless she is feeling poorly, she prefers to do her own shopping. I have also learned that the shopping is partly an excuse to socialize, because she almost always runs into someone she knows to chat with!

@madi2773 Yes. My husband died, fairly suddenly, about six years ago, and his youngest brother moved in with me--he's now my "caregiver" (custodian?) But that doesn't help either of us deal with his impatience, which he manages to the very best of his ability. This sucks, for both of us. And of course, it won't get any better.

I've always sworn that I won't go into residential care, ever, because the only two options locally in this small town are abysmal. But then, will I have the choice? I've told everyone who will listen that I want MAID if the care option should arise--I think my GP understands, don't know if anyone else does. Unsure even if I really do.....

Oh thank heaven--another kindred soul. My parents both had serious alcoholism, through all my childhood and my brother's. My brother died of cancer when he was 44--broke my heart. My mother never descended into dementia, but she was the milder alcoholic--I used to say that if she hadn't met my dad, she would have married some other toad, but he looked like a good bet when she met him. And her generation of woman rarely if ever left a marriage. Dad told her once that he figured he'd been an alcoholic from the time he picked up his first drink, at 14--lots of family tragedy, "stiff upper lip' family, so he was probably right. He had Korsikoff's (sp?) by the time he died, in a scuzzy retirement home, because he got kicked out of the good one, because he refused to accept that he could NOT smoke in the bathroom he shared with another resident--he always figured the rules were meant for other people, but not him.

And now I have a dx of early dementia, Alzheimer's variety. I can't tell anyone how devastating this is--I've always relied on my brain, which has been acute. I won't stick around for the later stages of this...

snippet.textDisplay:
My mom's mother in law (not my grandma) has been showing several signs of dementia, many of them severe and since she lives on her own most of the times, it is very hard to keep track of her. Me and my sister first noticed it on Christmas eve when she came to stay with us, she took a hard fall on the entry steps of our house, which she had visited the month before, back in November, stayed around for 30 minutes, getting to "know" the house. She fell to the ground and i tried helping her. The fall was particularly painful because she had a leg prosthetic from a fall back in July that messed up her leg completely.
What was supposed to be a two day stay turned into almost a week (24th of December to 30th). In that time, i was writing an essay for my university so i constantly locked myself in my room, and it really was depressing, my sister told me she had asked where i was several times in the time i was gone. But in the times i was not upstairs and took care of her with my sister, we would notice her telling a lot of stories from the past and go on tangents, not like when my mom with ADD goes on tangents, but she would bring up a completely unrelated topic out of nowhere, even if she could keep a reasoning line sometimes.
Another one is trying to keep track of the medications she has to take (she has diabetes and a lot of other conditions), her son tries to keep track of that but it's difficult since he works far from her. She is also very stubborn and when her son thought of taking her to a neurologist, he told us she didn't want to go because she has stuff to do at home. Another episode he told me and my mom was the soup episode. When he took her back home on the 30th, she wanted to welcome him to dinner and offered him some soup, opening the pan. The soup had mold growing in it, it stank and it was 8 days old, out of the freezer. and he told us she said to him it was made "before yesterday". It clearly wasn't, the soup was probably made before the 24th. She would oftentimes ask for her phone, i would give it to her, no questions, even though it was right by her side, along with her habit of getting lost in the house often. A more recent event that happened in the middle of march was the spaghetti incident which was similar to the soup incident but the spaghetti was 4 days old.
Thinking about it, she's been showing signs of dementia since July IMO, since that's where she took her worst fall and it has only been getting worse since there or maybe it's been going around unnoticed. Worst chapter was on the 30th too, since she registered a severe case of incontinence and when we made her change clothes, after cleaning the floor and the bathroom floor, my mom suggested giving her a bath (she hadn't showered since the 24th too), she clearly refused to do it and my mom gave up on it.
Going back to the spaghetti incident, she caught food poisoning from eating the spaghetti and had to stay with us again for two days, in that time, she vomited a lot, so much that after a few hours, her son took her to a healthcare center an hour away (after trying to feed her, she'd throw up in no time.). She had a hospital stay and is still in there and only now the doctors are stating she has Alzheimer's.
As you can see, English is clearly not my first language and i am mostly just a passerby to all of this, but since my mom and her BF are closer to her and are more well involved in her care, I'm now starting to watch these videos so i can try to pass pass some knowledge to them and maybe make them more empathic towards her, even if most of us do not find her to be a great person. Not only that but this video also makes me understand one of my biggest fears which is having dementia in the latter years (I'm 21) For these videos, I thank you.

Her memory exhibits certain quirks; she can vividly recall specific events, such as an incident where she accused a staff member at her assisted living facility of stealing her earrings. However, she struggles to remember daily activities, like having taken a shower just the day before. This inconsistency in her memory can be quite perplexing. One of the main challenges we face is her belief that no one trusts her regarding the alleged theft, which contributes to her feelings of isolation and increases her anxiety. Although she has a history of misplacing items that eventually reappear, this situation seems to cause her heightened distress. I have spent considerable time trying to reassure her and provide evidence of her safety, emphasizing that no one is entering her room. However, I often find myself getting frustrated and upset, leading to arguments with her.

This is one of the best vidoes I've watched when working with anyone who has some kind of memory loss. I forwarded it to some local home health companies and hopsice's requesting that ALL of their employees watch it.
I am so thankful for her videos.

My significant other has had several "silent strokes" which is a different type of stroke and difficult to diagnose. It occurs in the deep part of the brain which controls personality / emotions, decisions making, physical movements like balance and effects memory...
Whats was confusing is that he would be somewhat OK for a while then after a silent stroke its like being around someone who has severe dementia. I'm a retired RN so it frustrated me when no one couldn't figure out what was going on. They looked at me like I was overreacting and even making up his symptoms because he passed the standard cognitive tests given after a standard stroke. They finally did an MRI and CT which showed several areas in his deep brain which are permanently damaged. This is why over the last 3+ years he has been declining both physically and mentally. He is now end stage COPD from smoking with vascular dementia.

I am struggling with his inability to accept what happened. Maybe he can't understand it. Either way its taking a big toll on my health and sanity. I'm looking for support groups and I started counseling but I realized I need a counselor who understands dementia and how it affects us.

snippet.textDisplay: As fat as being slow and making time as well as cognitive function. Dressing can be an issue. I found that clothing that doesn't require buttons and zips is the way to go.  It also gives the person with dementia to be a little more independant and cuts back on issues such as assisting the caregiver who assists at the toilet like pulling up pants.  Pull-up nappies really helped me in looking after my mum in law and my own mother.  Tip, if you walk into a room in the morning and the person you are caring for is in a bad mood, smile, ask if they want a cup of tea or coffee and then walk out - do not linger, wait ten minutes and then re-enter. Most times you will get another mood you can deal with and if they want to chat, chat - open the curtains and distract with whatever is outside. Distraction is a good form of dealing with a situation.  If you are making their bed and you want them to stay seated - give them a bible and ask them to hold it for you - if not a bible and you have a clever dog like I had, ask them to throw a small ball for the dog to fetch.   These actions keep the person within range. Lastly, showering, washing and dignity.  Oft times caregivers forget about the patients dignity.  Cover those sentive areas with a towel and always ask if they can wash themselves in those areas first before going gungho. As a distraction, play music (this counteracts the noise of the water) they liked or as I would do, sing a song they loved so they can sing with you and as a final thing, no matter what - when you tuck them in tell them you love them and if permissible give them a hug and peck on the cheek.
